title: Why We Think We Know More Than We Do
gist: Matthew Hutson opens a breakdown of the Dunning-Kruger effect — done with David Dunning himself — using his own experience: after two decades of being complimented as a near-professional dancer at raves and parties, he was immediately the dunce in the back of a house-dance class. The effect remains often-cited and still-debated in both psychology and popular culture.

insights.claim: Two decades of being complimented and even mistaken for a professional while dancing at raves and parties left Matthew Hutson unprepared to be the least skilled student in a formal house-dance class — an illustration of how informal praise can mask the boundaries of one's competence.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hutson
insights.so_what: Feedback from an undemanding environment is the mechanism that inflates self-assessed skill; the audience matters more than the track record.
insights.quote: I hadn’t known what I didn’t know.
insights.locator: I immediately found myself the dunce

insights.claim: The Dunning-Kruger effect remains an often-cited and still-debated concept in both academic psychology and popular culture, rather than a settled finding.
insights.speaker: Matthew Hutson
insights.so_what: One of the most widely invoked heuristics about overconfidence is itself contested — treat casual citations of it as rhetoric, not evidence.
insights.quote: an often-cited and still-debated concept in both psychology and popular culture
insights.locator: My experience demonstrated what’s known as the Dunning-Kruger effect
